children.desc:
This section tracks GitHub star counts and push activity across 55 widely used open-source AI repositories, spanning frameworks like TensorFlow and PyTorch, inference tools like Ollama and llama.cpp, and newer agent projects like AutoGPT and browser-use. It ranks repositories by star count and tracks how many of them have been pushed to recently, as a proxy for which projects the developer community is actively building on.

Star counts and push dates are pulled from GitHub daily. Stars are a popularity and awareness signal, not a measure of code quality, security, or actual usage, and a repository can accumulate stars in a single event, a launch, a viral post, with little bearing on ongoing maintenance. Push activity only shows that a commit landed, not what changed or how significant it was.

As of September 5, 2026, the 55 tracked repositories hold 2,705,295 combined stars, growing by roughly 600 to 1,800 stars a day recently. TensorFlow leads with 198,841 stars, followed closely by AutoGPT at 187,142 and Ollama at 180,204. Forty-seven of the 55 repositories were pushed to within the last 7 days, and 49 within 30 days, indicating most tracked projects remain actively maintained. Agent-tooling repositories such as browser-use, 112,349 stars, and OpenHands, 86,228, now sit among the more-starred entries, alongside the established frameworks. Because stars accumulate steadily but rarely decline, the ranking also favors older, well-established projects even in periods when a newer entrant is seeing faster real-world adoption.
children.name: Repository Activity

children.desc:
This section tracks Hugging Face model activity: total download volume across roughly 16,363 tracked models, the most-downloaded individual models, and the license types those models are published under. It is meant to show what the open-model community is actually pulling and building with, as distinct from what gets announced or discussed.

Download totals are logged daily from mid-August 2026 onward. The figures count file downloads, which mix genuine usage with automated pipeline calls, CI jobs, and mirrored copies, so they should be read as an activity signal rather than a count of distinct users or deployments. A visible jump in the tracked total around August 21 to 22, from about 1.53 billion to 1.98 billion, looks like a change in tracking coverage rather than organic growth, so trend comparisons across that date are not reliable.

As of September 5, 2026, total downloads across tracked models stand at roughly 2.05 billion. The single most-downloaded model is not a flagship language model but a utility embedding model, sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2, with 255 million downloads, more than five times the second-place model. By license, apache-2.0 dominates with 7,036 of the tracked models, well ahead of MIT at 2,331 and models with no declared license at 1,872, underscoring how much of the ecosystem still runs on permissive open licensing. Downloads are also not deduplicated by user or organization, so a single team running automated pipeline jobs against a model can register as thousands of individual downloads with no distinct users behind them.
children.name: Hugging Face Trends

children.desc:
This section tracks measured uptime for 12 AI API providers, including Anthropic, OpenAI, Cohere, Groq, Cerebras, Deepgram, ElevenLabs, AssemblyAI, Stability AI, Baseten, Fireworks AI, and Lambda. For each provider it records a healthy or unhealthy status at each check and rolls that up into a healthy percentage over the tracked window, alongside a daily count of how many providers are currently healthy.

The status comes from automated checks against each provider's own reported status, run several times a day since mid-August 2026, not from independent synthetic testing of the live API endpoints. That means it reflects what providers disclose about their own availability, which can lag or understate real user-facing disruptions, and short blips between checks may not register at all. It is a directional reliability signal across providers, not a service-level guarantee.

As of September 5, 2026, all 12 tracked providers show healthy status, matching the pattern for most of the past week. Over the full tracked period, reliability is uneven. Lambda stands out as the clear laggard at 56.3 percent healthy across 142 checks, far below the rest of the field. OpenAI is next weakest at 88.5 percent, with Fireworks AI and Anthropic both around 95.9 percent. Six providers, including Groq, Deepgram, AssemblyAI, and Stability AI, recorded 100 percent healthy checks across the entire window.

children.desc: What can be lawfully measured about AI compute: quarterly capital expenditure from the seven companies whose capex is the buildout, read from their own XBRL facts on SEC EDGAR, plus GPU cloud service health and verified benchmark registries. Spot GPU availability has no public source - provider quota APIs report only one's own account - and this page says so rather than estimating.
children.name: Cloud GPU and Compute Telemetry

children.desc:
This section is meant to track capital flowing into AI companies by funding stage and sector. In its current form it reports two aggregate counts, a running total of funding-related filings and the number of distinct companies represented, without a breakdown by month or by individual round, investor, or sector.

The totals are checked daily and the series stretches back to mid-August 2026. However, the fields meant to hold recent-round detail and month-by-month breakdowns are both currently empty in the underlying data, so this section cannot yet tell readers which companies raised money, how large specific rounds were, who invested, or how funding is trending by sector or stage. It should be read as a coarse activity counter, not a funding-news feed, until that detail is populated.

As of September 5, 2026, the tracker shows 122 funding-related filings across 47 companies, up from 119 filings on August 14, a gain of just 3 filings over three weeks. That slow, steady pace suggests the underlying filing source updates infrequently, or that filing activity itself has been quiet in this window, but the aggregate count alone cannot distinguish between those two explanations. Readers looking for specific deal terms, investor names, or round sizes will not currently find them here and should treat the two totals as a directional signal only, not a funding-news record. Filling that gap would require deal-level sourcing this section does not yet ingest, rather than a change to how the two existing totals are calculated.
children.name: Funding Activity

children.desc:
This section tracks cumulative AI-related patent counts for 108 companies, ranking them by total portfolio size and charting how the combined total moves over time. It answers who is building the largest patent positions in AI, not who is inventing the most cutting-edge techniques right now, since raw filing counts favor large, long-established portfolios over newer, more selective filers.

The total is checked daily but only changes in step jumps every five to seven days, so it is best read as a periodically refreshed patent-database snapshot rather than a live daily count of new filings. Filing databases also lag actual invention by months given publication delays, and patent volume says nothing about which filings cover techniques that matter commercially or turn out to be defensible.

As of September 5, 2026, the tracked total stands at 312,470 AI-related patents across the 108 companies, up from 310,516 three weeks earlier, a gain of about 1,954 patents, or roughly 650 per week. Samsung leads by a wide margin with 108,943 patents, more than the next three companies combined, IBM at 69,827, Apple at 31,794, and Huawei at 27,442. Microsoft follows at 24,682. Further down, chip and model companies file far less by volume. NVIDIA holds 3,489, Meta 2,684, and Palantir 1,668, reflecting narrower but more targeted AI patent strategies. The count also tracks granted patents rather than pending applications, so it understates real activity for companies whose recent filings are still in prosecution and have not yet issued.

This section tracks open incidents reported on the status pages of 12 AI infrastructure and model providers, including Anthropic, OpenAI, Cohere, Lambda, Fireworks AI, Baseten, Deepgram, and ElevenLabs. It counts how many incidents each provider has open at a given time, not a curated list of disclosed security breaches, so it works as an operational health signal rather than a security news feed. Status pages are checked multiple times a day and logged daily, giving a running count back to mid-August 2026.

Because it draws on provider-published status pages, it will catch outages and provider-declared incidents, but it will miss anything a company does not post to its own status page, including disclosed vulnerabilities, data exposures, or research findings about model behavior. Read it as a proxy for provider reliability stress, not as a security-incident archive.

As of September 5, 2026, the tracker shows zero open incidents across all 12 providers, following a quieter stretch since late August. The busiest period was August 14 through 25, when 2 to 4 incidents were open concurrently most days, peaking at 4 on August 24. Lambda has been the most incident-prone provider by far, with incidents flagged on 62 of 142 checks, about 44 percent, versus 21 of 148 for OpenAI, 14 percent, and 18 of 148 for Fireworks AI, 12 percent. Cohere, Anthropic, Baseten, and Deepgram each cleared over 97 percent of checks incident-free.
